Part C · Chapter 2

Convolutional networks

Stacked filters that read a handwritten tag number, the part of the picture one cell can depend on, and where the reader fails

A filter finds one pattern. A convolutional network (CNN) stacks layers of filters, with pooling in between, so that later layers read patterns made from earlier ones. This chapter builds the stack, runs a trained network on a digit you draw, measures how much of the picture one cell can depend on, and counts the numbers that shared filters save. Shifted and turned digits then show where it fails.

You will need: filters, stride, padding and pooling (C1), softmax (A3) and the idea that backpropagation sets the weights (B4).

  1. From one filter to a stack

From one filter to a stack

Guess first. A 28 by 28 digit goes through a 3 by 3 convolution (stride 1, no padding) with 6 filters and a 2 by 2 max pool. The result goes through a second such convolution with 12 filters, another 2 by 2 max pool and a dense layer with 10 outputs. How wide are the maps before the dense layer, and about how many numbers must the network learn: hundreds, thousands or millions?

A convolutional network (CNN) is a list of layers applied in order. A convolution layer slides a bank of filters over its input and writes one map per filter. A max pool shrinks a map by keeping the largest value of a 2 by 2 block. A dense layer turns the last maps into ten scores, after flatten has unrolled them into one row. A layer's settings fix its output size and its count of numbers, so both can be computed before training.

  1. The table gives the output size and the numbers learned of the five layers; the coral box adds them up.
  2. Click the row of conv 2: the boxes below work out its output side, 11, and its 660 numbers.
  3. In that row change 12 filters to 24 and press Enter: the dense layer grows to 6,010 numbers and the total to 7,390.

The 12 maps before the dense layer are 5 by 5 and flatten unrolls them into 300 inputs, and the five layers have 3,730 numbers.

How it works

Follow the digit through the five layers. A convolution or pool with filter side \(k\), padding \(p\) and stride \(s\) turns an input of side \(n\) into an output of side \(\lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s \rfloor + 1\), where \(\lfloor\ \rfloor\) rounds down (the output-size formula). Conv 1 (\(k = 3\), \(p = 0\), \(s = 1\)) turns 28 into 26, and pool 1 (\(k = 2\), \(s = 2\)) halves it to 13. Conv 2 gives 11, and pool 2 gives \(\lfloor (11 - 2)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 5\), because 11 is odd and the last row and column are left out. The 12 maps of 5 by 5 flatten to 300 inputs.

A convolution layer with \(F\) filters over \(C_{\text{in}}\) input maps has \((k \cdot k \cdot C_{\text{in}} + 1) \cdot F\) numbers: \(k \cdot k \cdot C_{\text{in}}\) weights and one bias per filter. The dense layer has 300 weights and one bias per output, and a pool has no numbers to learn. The boxes below work out the three counts and add them to 3,730.

side 28 → 26 → 13 → 11 → 5conv, pool, conv, pool|60conv 1: (3×3×1+1)×6+660conv 2: (3×3×6+1)×12+3,010dense: (300+1)×10=3,730numbers learned

Analogy. A CNN is a line of inspectors: the first look for short edges, the next combine edges into curves, and the last decides which digit it is.

Where it breaks. No one assigns these jobs, because all filters start random and training adjusts them together by gradient descent. The first layer often ends up with edge-like filters, as here, but some filters are plain blurs, and later maps are not simply curves or loops (see the explaining chapter).

Quick quiz

A 3 by 3 conv layer with padding 1 and stride 1 turns 8 maps of 14 by 14 into 16 maps. What is the output size, and how many numbers does the layer learn?

The side stays 14, because \(\lfloor (14 + 2 - 3)/1 \rfloor + 1 = 14\). The layer learns \((3 \cdot 3 \cdot 8 + 1) \cdot 16 = 73 \cdot 16 = 1{,}168\) numbers.

Why does the dense layer have 300 inputs?

The last pool leaves 12 maps of 5 by 5, and 12 × 5 × 5 = 300. Flatten lists them in one row.

The whole network as one composition

The whole network is a composition of the layers. A superscript in square brackets numbers the layer.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}^{[1]} &= \mathrm{pool}\big(\mathrm{ReLU}(K^{[1]} * \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{[1]})\big) \\ \mathbf{h}^{[2]} &= \mathrm{pool}\big(\mathrm{ReLU}(K^{[2]} * \mathbf{h}^{[1]} + \mathbf{b}^{[2]})\big) \\ \mathbf{p} &= \mathrm{softmax}\big(W\,\mathrm{flat}(\mathbf{h}^{[2]}) + \mathbf{b}\big) \end{aligned} \]

  • \(\mathbf{x}\) is the 28 by 28 picture and \(\mathbf{h}^{[l]}\) is the stack of maps after layer \(l\) (6 maps of 13 by 13, then 12 maps of 5 by 5).
  • \(K^{[l]}\) contains the filters of layer \(l\). Here \(K\) is short for kernel, the filter of C1, and not the keys of attention. The star means slide and sum, as in C1. A filter in layer 2 spans all 6 maps of layer 1, so it has \(3 \cdot 3 \cdot 6\) weights.
  • \(\mathbf{b}^{[l]}\) is one bias per filter. \(W\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) are the weights (10 by 300) and biases of the dense layer.
  • \(\mathbf{p}\) is the vector of ten probabilities. Softmax is the function of A3.

Because the filters are reused at all positions, the picture side \(n\) does not appear in the count of a convolution layer. Only the count of the dense layer depends on the picture size, through its flattened input.

The same network in PyTorch

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class TagReader(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 6, 3)        # 28 -> 26, six 3 by 3 filters
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(6, 12, 3)       # 13 -> 11, twelve filters over six maps
        self.fc = nn.Linear(12 * 5 * 5, 10)    # 5 by 5 maps after the second pool
    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv1(x)), 2)
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv2(x)), 2)
        return self.fc(x.flatten(1))           # ten scores

net = TagReader()
print(net(torch.zeros(1, 1, 28, 28)).shape)
for name, p in net.named_parameters():
    print(f"{name:12s} {str(tuple(p.shape)):16s} {p.numel()}")
print("total", sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters()))
torch.Size([1, 10])
conv1.weight (6, 1, 3, 3)     54
conv1.bias   (6,)             6
conv2.weight (12, 6, 3, 3)    648
conv2.bias   (12,)            12
fc.weight    (10, 300)        3000
fc.bias      (10,)            10
total 3730

Training it

Training adds a loop. The loss is the cross-entropy of B3. The call loss.backward() runs the backward pass of B4 through the convolutions. A filter weight used at 676 positions receives the sum of the slopes from all of them. In the run printed below, two passes over the 60,000 training digits already gave 97.4% on the 10,000 test digits.

# X, y: 60,000 training digits (0..1, size (60000, 1, 28, 28)) and labels
# Xt, yt: the 10,000 test digits and labels
net = TagReader(); opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
for epoch in range(2):
    perm = torch.randperm(60000)
    for i in range(0, 60000, 128):
        idx = perm[i:i + 128]
        loss = F.cross_entropy(net(X[idx]), y[idx])      # softmax and log loss in one call
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    acc = (net(Xt).argmax(1) == yt).float().mean().item()
    print(f"pass {epoch + 1}: last loss {loss.item():.3f}, test accuracy {acc:.3f}")
pass 1: last loss 0.118, test accuracy 0.972
pass 2: last loss 0.045, test accuracy 0.974

The network of this chapter was trained for 10 passes with a learning-rate schedule. The training digits were shifted by up to 2 squares, turned by up to 10 degrees and zoomed between 0.9 and 1.1. In the run of data/train_cnn.py, this network reached 98.9% on the 10,000 test digits and the same network trained without these changed copies reached 98.7%. A dense network with one hidden layer of 128 units needs (784 + 1) × 128 + (128 + 1) × 10 = 101,770 numbers for the same digit. In my run (the script is not published), it reached 97.4% after 10 passes with the same optimiser and no tuning. That is one run per network, so the gap of 1.3 to 1.5 points is only a rough guide.

The buttons Add conv 3 by 3, Add max pool 2 by 2, Add dense layer and Remove last build other stacks. The chips at the top switch the input to a 64 by 64 colour crop or a 224 by 224 photo. Common mistakes

Debug tip. Conv2d expects input of size (batch, channels, height, width). A batch of grey digits has no channel, so add one with x[:, None], or the layer raises a size error. And cross_entropy wants raw scores. If you apply softmax first and then cross_entropy, the softmax runs twice. The first one squeezes the scores into the range 0 to 1. The second one then cannot give the right class a probability above 0.232 for ten classes, so the loss stays above 1.46.

Reading a handwritten tag

Guess first. You draw a 7, and the network answers with ten numbers, one per digit. What do the ten numbers add up to? And how many of them do you expect to be above 0.1?

A CNN reads in stages. The six filters of layer 1 write six maps, and pooling shrinks them. The twelve filters of layer 2 write twelve smaller maps, which pooling shrinks to 5 by 5. A dense layer computes one score per digit from these 300 numbers, and softmax turns the ten scores into ten probabilities that are positive and add up to 1.

  1. Draw a digit on the pad, or press a test button, and the maps and bars update. The small squares above the layer 1 maps are its filters, teal for positive weights and coral for negative.
  2. Click a bar and the boxes under the maps turn the score of that digit into its probability; the last box shows that the ten probabilities add up to 1.000.
  3. Press misread 9 as 5: 3 bars are above 0.1 (5 with 0.71, 9 with 0.16, 8 with 0.13), while any test button gives only one.

Draw here with the mouse or a finger

What the network sees

Probabilities. Click a bar for its working.

The layer 1 maps still look like the drawing, the smaller layer 2 maps do not, and the last step turns 300 numbers into ten probabilities that add up to 1.

How it works

Take the digit of the button misread 9 as 5. The network gives the digits 5, 9 and 8 the scores \(z_5 = 3.82\), \(z_9 = 2.35\) and \(z_8 = 2.10\); the other seven are no larger than \(-1.39\). The boxes under the figure subtract the largest score, 3.82, before taking exponentials, which leaves the probabilities unchanged. Then \(e^{z - 3.82}\) is 1.000, 0.230 and 0.179 for the three digits, and the sum over all ten is 1.416. So \(p_5 = 1.000/1.416 = 0.706\) and \(p_9 = 0.230/1.416 = 0.162\), and \(p_8\) is about 0.13: three probabilities are above 0.1.

\[ z_k = \mathbf{w}_k \cdot \mathbf{h} + b_k, \qquad p_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=0}^{9} e^{z_j}} \]

Here \(\mathbf{h}\) is the row of 300 numbers from the last maps, \(\mathbf{w}_k\) is the row of 300 weights of digit \(k\), \(b_k\) is its bias and \(z_k\) is its score. The exponential makes the ten values positive and gives a larger score a larger share, and dividing by their sum makes the shares add up to 1.

Common belief. A network that is right on 98.9% of the test digits knows what a digit is.

Why it fails. The 98.9% was measured on digits only. In a test with 2,000 images of random noise (pixel values drawn at random between 0 and 1), the network answered 8 for nearly all of them, with a probability above 0.9 for about 94%. The probabilities must add up to 1, so softmax has no way to say “none of these”.

Better account. A softmax probability is a share among the ten classes the network was trained on. It does not measure whether the picture is a digit at all.

Quick quiz

The scores are 2.0, 0.0 and −1.0 for three classes. What are the probabilities?

\(e^{2} = 7.389\), \(e^{0} = 1\), \(e^{-1} = 0.368\), and the sum is 8.757. The probabilities are 0.844, 0.114 and 0.042, and they add up to 1.

The network answers 8 for pure noise. Does that show that the noise resembles an 8?

Not necessarily. The weights were fitted to digits, and noise is outside that data. Some class must win, and softmax can turn its win into a high probability.

How this network was made

The network has 3,730 numbers. It was trained offline in PyTorch on the handwritten digits of C1 (MNIST, LeCun et al., 1998), then exported as weights, and it runs here in plain JavaScript in your browser. On the 10,000 MNIST test digits it was right 98.9% of the time in my run. It plays the part of the reader of tag numbers in SharkCam's logbooks.

Preparing a drawing like MNIST

MNIST digits fit a 20 by 20 box. They are placed in a 28 by 28 picture so that their centre of mass, the average position of the ink weighted by its value, is in the middle. The network was trained on such digits, with small random shifts, turns and zoom added. The box Centre and scale my drawing like MNIST does the same two steps to your drawing. Untick it, draw a small digit in one corner and compare.

The six filters of layer 1

The filters have some structure. Filters 2 and 5 compare the top and the bottom of the window: their top and bottom rows have weights of opposite sign. Filter 6 compares left and right. Filters 3 and 4 have mostly positive weights, so they act as blurs. Filter 1 is a dead unit (B1). None of its weights is larger in size than about 0.2 and its bias is −0.26, so the largest value it can reach before ReLU, for pixel values between 0 and 1, is about 0.06. ReLU left its map empty for the 20 digits loaded in the figure and, in a count of mine that is not in the published script, for all 10,000 test digits. This describes this trained network only. Another training run gives different filters.

The layer 2 maps

Layer 1 maps keep the layout of your drawing, so you can recognise it in them. Layer 2 maps have 11 by 11 cells (5 by 5 after pooling), and a cell covers a larger patch (the next section measures how large). A digit is hard to read in them. The dense layer multiplies the 300 numbers of the last maps by its weights and gets one score per digit.

Softmax in more detail

The score \(z_k\) is also called a logit, as in the softmax classifier, and the probabilities are the softmax of 0.7.

  • \(z_k\) is the score of digit \(k\), a dot product of its 300 weights \(\mathbf{w}_k\) with the flattened last maps, plus a bias \(b_k\).
  • \(p_k\) is the probability of digit \(k\). The ten values are positive and add up to 1 by construction.
  • The boxes under the figure subtract the largest score before taking the exponential. This does not change \(p_k\) and avoids overflow when scores are large, the usual practice in code (0.7).

The noise test

The noise test sent 2,000 images with pixel values drawn at random between 0 and 1 through the network. In my run the answer was 8 for all of them, with a probability above 0.9 for 94%. Repeated with other random images, the test gives 8 for 99.8% or more and a probability above 0.9 for 93% to 96%. Possible fixes are an extra class for “not a digit” and checks on the scores before softmax. Draw a scribble or a letter in the figure and see whether the answer is also confident. B9 shows what a network looks at when it makes a call like this.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. When a model works on test digits and fails on your own pictures, look at what it receives. Compare your 28 by 28 array with a test digit. Is the ink high and the paper 0 (white on black)? Is the digit about 20 squares tall and centred? Is the scale 0 to 1? A mismatch in one of these is a common cause of failure for a first deployed model. The panel “What the network sees” is that check.

In Python

In code, softmax subtracts the largest score first, as the boxes under the figure do, so large scores no longer overflow.

import numpy as np

def softmax(z):
    e = np.exp(z - z.max())            # subtract the largest score: same answer, no overflow
    return e / e.sum()

print(softmax(np.array([2.0, 0.0, -1.0])).round(3))
print(softmax(np.array([1000.0, 0.0, -1000.0])))   # exp(1000) overflows
[0.844 0.114 0.042]
[1. 0. 0.]

What one cell can see

Guess first. A cell, one number in a map of conv layer 2, reads a 3 by 3 patch of the maps that pool 1 wrote. How many pixels of the original 28 by 28 digit can its value depend on: 9, 16, 36 or 64?

The receptive field of a cell is the square of input pixels that can change its value, and \(r\) is its side. The jump \(j\) is the distance in input pixels between neighbouring cells of a map. A layer with filter or pool side \(k\) and stride \(s\) turns the receptive field \(r_{\text{in}}\) and the jump \(j_{\text{in}}\) of its input into \(r_{\text{out}} = r_{\text{in}} + (k-1)\,j_{\text{in}}\) and \(j_{\text{out}} = s\,j_{\text{in}}\).

  1. Click a cell in the map on the right, or use the arrow keys: the coral frame on the digit shows the pixels that cell can depend on, 8 by 8 for conv 2.
  2. Press Pool 2: the frame grows to 10 by 10, and the table under the figure lists \(r\) and \(j\) layer by layer.
  3. With the nudge test ticked, the figure measures the slope of the cell for the pixels of the frame, one at a time: how much the cell moves per unit change of the pixel. It shades the pixels teal, darker for larger slopes.

The digit you drew, with the receptive field in coral

The map. Click a cell, or use the arrow keys.

A conv 2 cell can depend on an 8 by 8 patch of the digit and a pool 2 cell on a 10 by 10 patch, and the influence inside the patch is uneven.

How it works

Work from the pixels to pool 2. For the picture itself \(r = 1\) and \(j = 1\). A conv 1 cell reads 3 by 3 pixels, so \(r = 3\) and \(j = 1\). A pool 1 cell reads 2 by 2 conv 1 cells, so \(r = 3 + (2-1) \cdot 1 = 4\) and \(j = 2\). A conv 2 cell reads 3 by 3 pool 1 cells, so \(r = 4 + (3-1) \cdot 2 = 8\), which answers the guess: 8 × 8 = 64 pixels. A pool 2 cell reads 2 by 2 conv 2 cells, so \(r = 8 + (2-1) \cdot 2 = 10\) and \(j = 4\).

\(r_{\text{out}} = 8\)a conv 2 cell=\(r_{\text{in}} = 4\)a pool 1 cell+\(k - 1 = 2\)gaps in a window of 3 cells×\(j_{\text{in}} = 2\)pool 1 cells are 2 pixels apart

A window of \(k\) cells has \(k - 1\) gaps of \(j_{\text{in}}\) pixels, and its last cell adds its own \(r_{\text{in}}\). A pool or a stride raises the jump, so conv 2 adds \(2 \cdot 2 = 4\) pixels where conv 1 added \(2 \cdot 1 = 2\).

Common belief. A cell reads all pixels of its receptive field equally.

Why it fails. In a nudge test on 20 test digits, I took the 5 strongest pool 2 cells per digit. The medians over these 100 cells were 43% of the frame's pixels with a slope above a tenth of the cell's largest slope, and 68% of the summed absolute slopes in the middle 6 by 6 (about a third of the frame).

Better account. The receptive field is the upper limit of what a cell can depend on. The effective receptive field, the pixels that change the value by a noticeable amount, is usually smaller and concentrated in the middle (Luo et al., 2016).

Quick quiz

Three stacked 3 by 3 convolutions with stride 1 and no pooling: what is the receptive field?

\(r = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7\). A layer adds \((3-1) \cdot 1 = 2\). A single 7 by 7 filter has the same receptive field.

Why is the receptive field of conv 2 (8) bigger than \(3 + 3 - 1 = 5\)?

Pool 1 lies between the layers and doubles the jump. The conv 2 window spans two gaps of 2 pixels, so it adds \(2 \cdot 2 = 4\), not 2, to the 4 pixels of a pool 1 cell.

How the figure measures influence

The figure uses the digit from the drawing pad above. Pick a layer, then click a cell in the map. The coral frame shows which input pixels the cell can depend on, and the equation boxes give its size. With the nudge test ticked, the figure also changes the pixels in the frame by 0.1 up and down, one at a time, and measures how much the cell moves. This estimates a slope, in the sense of 0.6, by central differences as in gradient checking. The status line counts the pixels of the frame with a slope above a tenth of the largest slope. For the test 4 that is loaded at the start, it reports 29 of 64 pixels for conv 2 and 29 of 100 for pool 2. The frame answers “could this pixel matter?”, and the nudge test answers “does it, for this picture?”. The coral frame is the full receptive field, and the teal pixels are the ones whose nudge changes the cell the most.

The recursion and its symbols

\[ \begin{aligned} r_{\text{out}} &= r_{\text{in}} + (k - 1)\, j_{\text{in}} \\ j_{\text{out}} &= s\, j_{\text{in}} \\ \text{first input pixel of cell } i &= i \cdot j_{\text{out}} \end{aligned} \]

  • \(r_{\text{in}}\) is the receptive field of one cell of the layer's input (1 for the picture itself), and \(r_{\text{out}}\) that of one cell of its output.
  • \(k\) and \(s\) are the filter or pool size and the stride. \(j_{\text{in}}\) is the jump of the input map in pixels.
  • Why it works: a window of \(k\) cells covers \((k-1)\) gaps of \(j_{\text{in}}\) pixels, plus the receptive field of one cell at its end.
  • Padding shifts the frame by the padding but does not change its size. This network has no padding, so the frame starts at \(i \cdot j_{\text{out}}\).

The nudge test in numbers

I nudged the pixels of the frame for the 5 cells with the largest values in the layer, separately for the 20 example test digits, which makes 100 cells per layer. For conv 2, the median cell had 64% of its frame's pixels above a tenth of its largest slope, and the middle 4 by 4 of the frame, a quarter of its pixels, had 42% of the total slope (the sum of the absolute slopes). For pool 2 the median cell had 43% of its frame's pixels above that level, and the middle 6 by 6, about a third of its pixels, had 68%. A slope can be small or zero inside a frame because the filter weights differ, ReLU outputs zero where its input is negative, and a max pool passes on only the largest value of a block.

Why this matters for SharkCam

A shark may fill 300 pixels of a 640 pixel photo. A cell with a 10 by 10 receptive field can depend only on a patch much smaller than the shark, such as a bit of skin or a tooth. To tell a shark from a ray, a late layer often needs a receptive field about as large as the animal. Networks raise it by stacking many layers and by pooling and strides, which raise the jump. The cost is that a deep cell mixes in a large patch, so the position of a detail becomes less certain.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a CNN fails on large objects but works on small ones, one possible cause is a receptive field of the last conv layer that is small compared with the object, so compare the two. If the field is much smaller, options are a pool or a stride earlier, one more layer, or a smaller photo.

In Python

The recursion is four lines of code. It reproduces the table above.

layers = [("conv1", 3, 1), ("pool1", 2, 2),
          ("conv2", 3, 1), ("pool2", 2, 2)]       # (name, k, s)
r, j = 1, 1                  # one input pixel: receptive field 1, jump 1
for name, k, s in layers:
    r = r + (k - 1) * j      # k cells span k - 1 gaps of j pixels
    j = j * s
    print(f"{name}: receptive field {r} x {r}, jump {j}")
conv1: receptive field 3 x 3, jump 1
pool1: receptive field 4 x 4, jump 2
conv2: receptive field 8 x 8, jump 2
pool2: receptive field 10 x 10, jump 4

Why sharing filters saves numbers

Guess first. A conv layer with six 3 by 3 filters on a 28 by 28 digit has 60 numbers. A dense layer that writes the same six maps of 26 by 26 from the 784 pixels needs how many: about 6,000, about 600,000, or about 3 million?

In a dense layer an output has a weight for all inputs. Local connectivity cuts this to a small patch of the input. A locally connected layer keeps separate weights at separate output positions, while a convolution layer uses weight sharing: one set per filter, used at all positions. So locality cuts the weights per output to one patch, and sharing cuts the weight sets to one per filter.

  1. The bars count the numbers one layer needs to write the same maps from the same picture, on a log axis. At the start the dense layer needs 3.18 million, the locally connected layer 40,560 and the convolution 60.
  2. Press Photo: 224 by 224, 3 channels, 64 filters: the dense bar climbs to 483 billion (about 1.9 TB as 32-bit floats, says the box under the plot) while the convolution needs 1,792.
  3. Drag Picture side n and watch the dense bar change while the convolution bar stays where it is.

On the 28 by 28 digit the three layers need 3,183,960, 40,560 and 60 numbers, and on a 224 by 224 photo with 64 maps the dense layer needs about 483 billion.

How it works

Count the layer that reads the digit. The digit has side \(n = 28\) and \(C_{\text{in}} = 1\) channel. The layer has \(F = 6\) filters of side \(k = 3\) and no padding, so its maps have side \(m = 26\) and it writes \(26 \cdot 26 \cdot 6 = 4{,}056\) output squares. A dense layer gives an output square one weight per input plus a bias, \((784 + 1) \cdot 4{,}056 = 3{,}183{,}960\) numbers. A locally connected layer gives it only a 3 by 3 patch, so \(3 \cdot 3 + 1 = 10\) numbers and \(10 \cdot 4{,}056 = 40{,}560\) in all. A convolution shares those 10 numbers across the squares of a map, so it needs \(10 \cdot 6 = 60\).

\[ \begin{aligned} N_{\text{dense}} &= (n^2 C_{\text{in}} + 1)\, m^2 F \\ N_{\text{local}} &= (k^2 C_{\text{in}} + 1)\, m^2 F \\ N_{\text{conv}} &= (k^2 C_{\text{in}} + 1)\, F \end{aligned} \]

The dense count multiplies the \(n^2 C_{\text{in}}\) inputs of the whole picture by the \(m^2 F\) outputs. The locally connected count replaces the whole picture by the \(k^2 C_{\text{in}}\) inputs of a patch. The convolution count drops the factor \(m^2\), because one filter is used at all \(m^2\) positions.

Analogy. Weight sharing is one stamp pressed at many places on a page, instead of a different stamp for another place.

Where it breaks. A stamp gives the same mark wherever it is pressed, so a filter responds to a pattern in the same way at any position. Sharing assumes that a pattern means the same wherever it appears. That is true for a stroke in a digit and partly false for a photo from SharkCam's dive camera, where the sky is at the top and the sand at the bottom. The map still shows where a pattern was, because the cell that responds marks the position, and the dense layer at the end can use it.

Quick quiz

A conv layer has 3 by 3 filters, 16 input channels and 32 filters. How many numbers does it learn, and does the picture size change the answer?

\((3 \cdot 3 \cdot 16 + 1) \cdot 32 = 145 \cdot 32 = 4{,}640\). The picture size does not enter, so the count is the same for a 28 by 28 or a 224 by 224 input.

Why is the locally connected layer 40,560 and not 60?

An output square has its own 10 numbers (9 weights and a bias), and there are 4,056 output squares (6 maps of 26 by 26). That gives 40,560. The convolution shares 10 numbers per filter across all squares, so it has 60 for 6 filters.

Symbols

The three rows of equation boxes follow from counting weights. A dense layer connects all \(n \cdot n \cdot C_{\text{in}}\) inputs to all \(m \cdot m \cdot F\) outputs, plus one bias per output. Here \(m\) is the side of an output map and \(F\) the number of maps. They are not the number of examples or the Fisher information. A locally connected layer connects an output to only \(k \cdot k \cdot C_{\text{in}}\) inputs, but keeps separate weights for separate output squares, so it needs \((k^2 C_{\text{in}} + 1) \cdot m^2 F\). A convolution uses one set of weights per filter for all positions.

  • \(n\) is the side of the input and \(C_{\text{in}}\) its number of channels; \(m\) is the side of an output map and \(F\) the number of maps (filters).
  • \(k\) is the filter side. With same padding and stride 1, \(m = n\). With no padding, \(m = n - k + 1\).
  • The ratio \(N_{\text{dense}} / N_{\text{conv}}\) is about \(n^2 m^2 / k^2\): it grows with the fourth power of the picture side.

A second example: the photo

Photo: \(n = 224\), \(C_{\text{in}} = 3\), same padding, \(F = 64\), \(m = 224\). The dense layer has \(150{,}529 \times 3{,}211{,}264 \approx 4.8 \times 10^{11}\) numbers, which is about 1.9 terabytes as 32-bit floats. A layer of that size is impractical to store and to train. The convolution has \(28 \times 64 = 1{,}792\) numbers.

What sharing costs

The savings have a price. A convolution layer gives the same response to the same patch at any position (apart from the effect of padding at the edges), so its filter weights cannot depend on position. The position of a patch is still in the map, as the place of the cell that responds, and the dense layer at the end can use it, because it reads fixed positions in the flattened maps. CS231n (Karpathy and others) names the same limit for centred faces, where a locally connected layer can be better.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Count the numbers before you train: sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters()). If a small CNN has millions, the dense layer after flatten is a common cause. Without the two pools, the digit reader would flatten 12 maps of 24 by 24. That is 6,912 inputs and 69,130 numbers in the dense layer, which is 23 times more than now.

In Python

The three counts are one short function.

def counts(n, c_in, F, k, same=False):
    m = n if same else n - k + 1       # side of an output map
    outs = m * m * F                   # output squares in all maps
    dense = (n * n * c_in + 1) * outs  # an output reads all inputs
    local = (k * k * c_in + 1) * outs  # a patch, separate weights per square
    conv = (k * k * c_in + 1) * F      # a patch, one shared set per filter
    return dense, local, conv

print(counts(28, 1, 6, 3))
print(counts(224, 3, 64, 3, same=True))
(3183960, 40560, 60)
(483388358656, 89915392, 1792)

Where the reader fails

Guess first. A digit reader with shared filters and pooling layers was trained on centred digits only. The whole test set of 10,000 digits is moved 3 squares (pixels) to the right, or turned by 30 degrees. In either case, will its accuracy stay above 95%?

A convolution layer is equivariant to shifts: if the input moves, its maps move with it. The final answer is invariant to a shift when it stays the same after the input moves. The digit reader is not invariant by construction, because its dense layer reads fixed positions of the last maps. Training on shifted, turned or otherwise changed copies of the examples (data augmentation) can teach the network some invariance.

  1. Drag Move right to 3 squares and hover the curves: the navy one (trained on centred digits only) is at 87.9% and the teal one (trained with small shifts, turns and zoom) at 95.7%.
  2. Drag to 5 squares: the 7 on the left is still read as 7 (probability 0.98), but the teal curve is at 70.6% and the navy one at 44.0% of the 10,000 test digits.
  3. Press Turn and drag to 30 degrees: the navy curve is at 84.1% and the teal one at 85.9%.

The test digit after the change

Moving the test set 3 squares lowers a network trained on centred digits from 98.7% to 87.9%, and training with small shifts, turns and zoom lifts that result to 95.7%.

How it works

A shift of 3 squares. When the input moves by \(d\) pixels, a map whose cells are \(j\) pixels apart moves by \(d/j\) cells. A shift by part of a cell cannot give a shifted copy of the map. The dense layer after pool 2 also multiplies fixed positions of the last maps by fixed weights, so ink in new positions meets weights fitted to ink elsewhere, and the answer can change.

\(d = 3\)input shift, pixels÷\(j\) = 1, 2, 2, 4jump of conv 1, pool 1, conv 2, pool 2=3, 1.5, 1.5, 0.75shift of the maps, in cells

Training can teach tolerance. The teal network saw shifts of up to 2 squares, turns of up to 10 degrees and zoom between 0.9 and 1.1; the navy network was trained without these changes. Turns beyond 10 degrees were in neither training set, and the two turning curves stay within 2.5 points of one another (at 40 degrees, 67.9% against 65.9%).

Common belief. A CNN is invariant to where the object is, because it uses the same filter at all positions.

Why it fails. Equivariance is a property of the convolution layers. Invariance of the final answer is a separate property, and the dense layer is a likely place where it is lost: the navy curve falls to 87.9% at 3 squares.

Better account. Convolution gives equivariance, pooling a little tolerance, and training on shifted copies of the examples can add more.

Quick quiz

The conv 1 maps of a digit that is moved by 3 squares are shifted copies. Why can the answer still change?

The last layer is dense and reads fixed positions. The same ink in different positions meets different weights, and training on centred digits did not show it such positions.

What would you add to the training set to make the reader tolerate a 5 square shift?

Copies of the digits shifted by up to 5 squares. Fitting on those examples can teach the network the tolerance.

Go deeper reading the figure, wrap-around, debugging, code about 2 min

Reading the figure

The left panel shows the network of this chapter (trained with small shifts, turns and zoom) on one test digit, while the chart is the average over 10,000 digits, so a single digit can be read right where the average is poor. Both curves were measured on all 10,000 test digits, with one trained network per kind. The coral dotted line marks the setting of the slider. Turns use bilinear sampling with zeros outside the picture.

The shift wraps round the edge

The shift in this figure wraps round the edge, as torch.roll does: ink pushed off the right edge returns on the left. In a count of mine on the test set, which is not part of the published script, some ink wrapped for 6% of the test digits at 3 squares, 30% at 5 squares and 79% at 8 squares. The curves beyond about 4 squares therefore measure a different test than a plain slide would. A shift of 3 squares in the input is less than one cell of pool 2 (0.75 cell), and for the network trained on centred digits it can still move the ink into positions that were rare in its training digits.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. When a model does well on the test set and badly in the field, a common first suspect is a difference in position, size, lighting or colour between the two. Make a test set that applies one of those changes at a time, as this figure does, and measure which one hurts. That tells you which augmentation to add.

In Python

The same test in code, for the two-pass net of the first section, which was trained on digits without shifts. It gives 97.4%, 93.8% and 59.4% for 0, 2 and 4 squares. One run of a small network, so the numbers are a rough guide.

for dx in (0, 2, 4):
    right = (net(torch.roll(Xt, dx, dims=3)).argmax(1) == yt)
    print(f"moved right by {dx} squares: test accuracy {right.float().mean():.3f}")
moved right by 0 squares: test accuracy 0.974
moved right by 2 squares: test accuracy 0.938
moved right by 4 squares: test accuracy 0.594

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory Two ways to see a 7 by 7 patch: one 7 by 7 convolution, or three stacked 3 by 3 convolutions with stride 1. Show that both have a receptive field of 7. With \(C\) channels in and out and no biases, how many weights does the layer or stack use? Which is smaller, and by how much for \(C = 32\)?

    Hint

    One filter has \(k \cdot k \cdot C\) weights and there are \(C\) filters, so a layer has \(k^2 C^2\) weights.

  2. theory A network reads a 32 by 32 colour photo. Its layers are, in order: conv 5 by 5 with 16 filters and same padding. Max pool 2 by 2. Conv 3 by 3 with 32 filters and no padding. Max pool 2 by 2. Flatten. Dense 10. Give the side of the map after the layers, the number of numbers learned in the layers and the total.

  3. theory A dense layer writes 16 maps of 64 by 64 from a 64 by 64 RGB crop. A convolution with 3 by 3 filters (same padding) writes the same maps. Compute \(N_{\text{dense}}\), \(N_{\text{local}}\) and \(N_{\text{conv}}\), and the ratio of dense to conv.

  4. theory Explain why shifting the input of a convolution layer by one pixel shifts its output by one cell. Then explain why a dense layer after flatten breaks that property. What does max pooling with block size 2 do to a shift of one pixel?

Practice

  1. practice Build torchvision.models.resnet18() without weights. Pass a zero tensor of size (1, 3, 224, 224) through conv1, maxpool, layer1, layer2, layer3 and layer4 in turn and print the sizes. Compare the first two with the output-size formula, and print the number of numbers in the layers.

  2. practice Train the TagReader for 3 passes. Then measure its test accuracy when the test digits are moved right by 0 to 6 squares with torch.roll. Plot or print the curve and compare it with the chart above.

  3. practice Replace all max pools in the TagReader by a convolution with stride 2 (so that the map sizes stay the same). How does the number of parameters change, and what accuracy do you get after 3 passes?

Think deeper

  1. open Turn the test digits by 180 degrees and look at which digits the network confuses. Which pairs would you expect, and why? What does this say about asking a CNN to read a tag that is held upside down?

  2. open SharkCam has to find sharks that are 40 to 400 pixels wide. How do the receptive field of the last layer and the pooling layers interact with the size of the shark? Describe two designs that could handle several sizes and what you would measure to choose between them.

  3. open The reader answers 8 for random noise. Propose two ways to make it answer “not a digit” for such inputs, and a test set that would show whether it works.

Come back later

Try these after two days and again after a week. Say the answer aloud before you open it.

A 5 by 5 conv layer with stride 2 and padding 2 reads a 28 by 28 map. What is the output side, and how does a 2 by 2 max pool with stride 2 change it? (C1)

Conv: \(\lfloor (28 + 4 - 5)/2 \rfloor + 1 = \lfloor 13.5 \rfloor + 1 = 14\). The pool then gives \(\lfloor (14-2)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 7\).

In the digit reader, one weight of a conv 1 filter is used at 26 × 26 positions. How many terms are added up in its slope for one training digit, and why? (B4, a value used twice)

There are 676 terms, one per position. A weight used several times has one path to the loss per use, and the slopes of the paths add up. The slope is then averaged over the batch.

Batch norm (B6) stores a mean and variance per channel and uses them at test time. For a CNN, the average runs over the batch and all positions of one channel. Why is that a natural choice for conv layers, given weight sharing?

All positions of a channel come from the same filter, so they have the same meaning and can share one mean and one variance. The statistics then need as many numbers as channels, not as many as squares.
